title: Anger at home
hookLine: the people closest often get the worst
tomorrow: a shop, a full cart, and Maya's grandma. what does she say?

lines: WHY AM I NICEST TO STRANGERS?
cards: On the road, Simran handled it. At home, two days later, she doesn't. She's up late on an essay, and Bebe, propped on the couch, asks for the third time where her reading glasses went.
Simran snaps: I don't know, Bebe, I'm busy! It comes out loud and sharp, in a voice she'd never use with a stranger. The house goes quiet.
Bebe finds the glasses on her own head and says nothing at all, which is worse. Earlier that day she was patient with a rude caller at her weekend job, polite the whole time.
Simran texts Maya from the hallway: why am I nicest to people I barely know?

teach.h: FARID, ANG 1382: ANGER AS A SICKNESS.
teach.b: Sheikh Farid saw this pattern long ago. His saloks in the Guru Granth Sahib are short and sharp.
On ang 1382 he says, in paraphrase: do good even to the one who does you wrong, and don't let anger fill your mind; then the body won't fall sick, and you'll have everything.
Notice he puts anger in the body again, as a sickness.

On ang 1384 he gives a cure in three parts: humility is the word, forbearance is the virtue, and sweet speech is the priceless mantra. Here's why home gets the worst of us. With strangers we're on guard.

teach.h: AT HOME, THE GUARD COMES DOWN.
teach.b: At home we put the guard down, which is the whole point of home, and the thief walks in through the open door. Farid's answer isn't to put the guard back up and be stiffly polite to our own family.
It's to make softness the habit, so it's still there when we're tired.
Softly at home doesn't mean silent, and it doesn't mean never disagreeing. It means the volume and the edge come down, especially with the people who'll still be there in the morning.
Simran goes back to the couch and sits on the floor by Bebe's boot. I'm sorry I yelled, she says, quietly. Bebe pats her head.
Then she asks for tea, with extra ginger.

how: Sikhs read Sheikh Farid's saloks, included in the Guru Granth Sahib, as guidance on anger and humility; the Gurbani ideal of sweet, humble speech applies at home as much as anywhere.

o: anger that only shows up in large families
anger that lands on the people closest to us
a fair way to show family how you really feel

games.q: the thief at home — tap the pairs.
p: his saloks are in the Guru Granth
don't let anger fill the mind

s: family can take it, so home is the safe place to let anger out
Farid calls anger a sickness; at home the guard is down, so softness needs to be a habit.
Sheikh Farid's words are part of the Guru Granth Sahib
his saloks are in it, including ang 1382 and 1384.
softly at home means never disagreeing with your family
it means the volume and the edge come down, not that you stop saying what's true.

games.q: you're exhausted after work. your brother asks, for the third time, if you've seen his charger. the sharp answer is ready. what fits today's lesson?
o: drop the volume and the edge, and answer him softly.
say nothing at all, so the anger can't come out.
tell him firmly to stop asking you things tonight.
games.why: softly at home isn't silence or a lecture. Farid's cure: humility, forbearance, sweet speech, as a habit that's there when you're tired.

practice: Say one ordinary sentence out loud at your usual speed, the kind you'd say at dinner. Then say it again at half the volume and a little slower, and listen to how it lands.
Let that softer voice be the one you sit with as you breathe.

wordCard.voice: Anger at home. The thief that walks in when the guard comes down, and the soft voice that keeps the door.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Farid, the Sufi poet Sheikh Farid, whose saloks are in the Guru Granth Sahib.

carryVoice: Softly at home: the people closest to us get the gentlest voice we have. Goodnight, gently.

sources.ref: Ang 1382 (Salok Sheikh Farid: fareedaa buray daa bhalaa kar gusaa man na hadhaae; dehee rog na lagaee palai sabh kichh paae), paraphrased
Ang 1384 (Salok Sheikh Farid: nivan so akhar khavan gun jihbaa maneeaa mant), paraphrased
